'''Commander Shepard''' is the [[player character]] in the ''[[Mass Effect]]'' video game series by [[BioWare]] (''[[Mass Effect (video game)|Mass Effect]]'', ''[[Mass Effect 2]]'', and ''[[Mass Effect 3]]'').

A veteran soldier of the Systems Alliance Navy, an N7 graduate of the Interplanetary Combatives Training (ICT) military program, and the first human Citadel Council Spectre, Shepard works to stop the [[Reapers (Mass Effect)|Reapers]], a sentient machine race dedicated to wiping out all advanced organic life. Shepard is neither a [[hero]], nor a [[villain]];<ref group=note>Paragon or Renegade morality system game mechanics</ref> depending upon players' choices and actions, Shepard is the abstaining factor that acts as both on occasion and will take whatever action is deemed necessary when presented with impossible scenarios.

Shepard's gender, [[Character class|class]], first name and facial appearance are chosen and customized by the player. The default male Shepard's face and body were modelled after Dutch [[Model (profession)|model]] [[Mark Vanderloo]], while [[Mark Meer]] provided the voice for the male Shepard. [[Jennifer Hale]] voiced the female Shepard. Since the player can choose the gender of Shepard, much of the dialogue revolving around the character is gender-neutral with only a few exceptions. In some other ''Mass Effect'' media, Shepard is pre-determined as a male character and referred to as such.

The character is inspired by and named after American astronaut [[Alan Shepard]]. Shepard's armor developed over the series and was originally intended to be red-and-white. Most promotional material for the series focused on the male Shepard, due to the studio's desire for a single identifiable hero, though both versions of the character were given equal priority during development. Various merchandise has been made, including several figurines. Shepard has made cameo appearances in other [[Electronic Arts]] games and is referenced in ''[[Mass Effect: Andromeda]]''.

==Concept and creation==
[[BioWare]] wanted players to feel special and empowered right from the start. Unlike other [[Role-playing video game|role-playing game]] protagonists, they felt Shepard should not be an entirely blank character for the player to create, in order to create a more "intense" experience; with the first ''Mass Effect'' being more cinematic than other BioWare video games, they felt they needed an "extra bit" with a sense of a specific flavor that can be caused by a memorable character, such as ''[[Star Trek]]''{{'}}s [[Captain Kirk]] or  ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]''{{'}}s [[Jack Bauer]].<ref name="ME Interview"/> Project director [[Casey Hudson]] also cited ''24'' as an influence on the kinds of morally ambiguous decisions presented to the player throughout the game's narrative.<ref name="TechRadar oral history">{{cite web |last=Bailes |first=Jon |title=Mass Effect: The oral history of a game-changing RPG |url=https://www.techradar.com/features/mass-effect-the-oral-history-of-a-game-changing-rpg |work=TechRadar |date=6 November 2022 |access-date=29 September 2026}}</ref>

The team decided that the player-created protagonist needed at least a fixed surname so that other characters could address the protagonist naturally in voiced dialogue. They wanted a name that was both "all-American" and common, which led them to start looking at the original seven astronauts. [[Alan Shepard]] was chosen due to fitting with the idea of "their" Shepard, being tough and respected, and fitting in with the character being the first human Spectre – Alan Shepard being the first American in space.<ref name="Hudson Interview"/>

Shepard's physical performance was developed separately from the character's facial appearance. Lead cinematics animator Shane Welbourn recalled that an actor initially hired for [[motion capture]] had recently injured his back, producing movements that did not suit the military character the team wanted. Welbourn subsequently performed most of Shepard's motion-captured movements himself.<ref name="TechRadar oral history"/>

===Appearance and design===
Early armor designs for Shepard in the first ''Mass Effect'' were comparatively close-fitting or skintight; following fan feedback, Shepard's armor became progressively bulkier over the course of the series to give off an imposing presence.<ref name="Art direction">{{cite web |title=Q&A: The Art Direction of Mass Effect |url=https://primagames.com/eguides/mass-effect-3-eguide/extras/collectors-edition/qa-the-art-direction-of-mass-effect |website=Prima Games |at=Interview with Derek Watts |access-date=September 29, 2026}}</ref> The armor became piece-based in ''[[Mass Effect 2]]'' to stress the character's [[silhouette]], as well as making them look "stronger and able to take more punishment".<ref name="Universe Art"/> Despite this, the colors, as well as other elements of the armor and the commander's appearance, are customisable in ''Mass Effect 2''.<ref name="Iron Man"/> 

The color of Shepard's default armor was originally red-and-white, but this was changed to charcoal grey, with a red-and-white stripe and the N7 logo, as Shepard looked too much like a medic.<ref name="Universe Art"/> Art director Derek Watts recalled that the N7 mark originated from a logo he had seen on ski equipment. After it was added to an early design, the team repeatedly retained it until the insignia and stripe became identifying elements of Shepard's appearance.<ref name="Art direction"/> The red stripe in the N7 logo is meant to symbolise the blood the character must sacrifice to save the galaxy.<ref name="1 Art"/>

For the character customization at the start of the game, they focused on "quality and realism". In order to test out the customisation system, the team made various [[celebrity look-alike]]s to ensure it offered a wide enough variety.<ref name="CCS"/> The team considered several approaches considered for the default male Shepard's face. Watts recalled that one experimental version used [[George Clooney]]'s face as a reference; although Clooney was not intended to become the final model, the short hair and square jaw helped establish the direction of the character.<ref name="TechRadar oral history"/> Watts later encountered photographs of [[Mark Vanderloo]] and tested his likeness on the existing Shepard model. He felt Vanderloo provided a less exaggerated action-hero appearance and a look that was difficult to associate with any single contemporary ethnicity, which suited the series' future setting.<ref name="Art direction"/><ref name="TechRadar oral history"/> Vanderloo's likeness was subsequently used for the default male Shepard.<ref>{{cite web |first=Adam |last=Salandra |title=Then And Now: The Male Supermodels Of The 1990s |url=http://www.newnownext.com/male-supermodels-90s/08/2017/ |publisher=newnownext.com |date=22 August 2017 |access-date=24 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190717063032/http://www.newnownext.com/male-supermodels-90s/08/2017/ |archive-date=17 July 2019}}</ref>

During the development of the first game, the female Shepard was given equal importance as the male counterpart; unique lines were written for her as well as a unique romance option. An early animation test for the first game used a female Shepard model.<ref name="animtest"/> Hudson described the female Shepard as a strong character in her own right rather than a caricature of a female role-playing protagonist, emphasizing that she could be sensitive while remaining confident and assertive.<ref name="CCS"/> Although both versions of Shepard were playable from the first game, the male default Shepard initially dominated the series' promotional material. According to marketing director David Silverman, BioWare decided during the development of ''Mass Effect 3'' to give the female Shepard greater visibility, including her own trailer and a place on the collector's edition packaging.<ref name="FemShep marketing">{{cite web |last=Francis |first=Tom |title=BioWare will give female Shepard her own trailer and place on Mass Effect 3's box |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/bioware-will-give-female-shepard-her-own-trailer-and-place-on-mass-effect-3s-box/ |work=PC Gamer |date=16 June 2011 |access-date=29 September 2026}}</ref>

[[File:FemShepandCo.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|alt=Six versions of the female Commander Shepard arranged in two rows of three, wearing the same N7 armour but with different facial features and hairstyles.|The six designs used for BioWare's initial 2011 vote to select the default female Shepard for ''Mass Effect 3''.]]
While the default female face only changed slightly between the first and second game,<ref name="To Appear"/>  the female Shepard's default appearance for ''Mass Effect 3'' was substantially redesigned. BioWare placed six proposed design online and invited [[Fan (person)|fans]] to vote for their preferred version through [[Facebook]].<ref name=Choose>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.gameinformer.com/b/news/archive/2011/07/24/bioware-lets-fans-choose-female-shepard-39-s-new-look.aspx |title=Bioware Lets Fans Choose Female Shepard's New Look |author=Tim Turi |date=July 24, 2011 |magazine=[[Game Informer]] |access-date=May 13, 2013 |archive-date=December 3, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141203220441/http://www.gameinformer.com/b/news/archive/2011/07/24/bioware-lets-fans-choose-female-shepard-39-s-new-look.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="What Does"/> The six candidates had been selected from a larger collection of concepts produced during development.<ref name="Unused and Unseen">{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/the-many-unused-and-unseen-faces-of-femshep-5892374 |title=The Many Unused and Unseen Faces of FemShep |author=Luke Plunkett |date=March 12, 2012 |work=Kotaku |access-date=May 13, 2013 |archive-date=June 18, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120618014535/http://kotaku.com/5892374/the-many-unused-and-unseen-faces-of-femshep |url-status=live }}</ref> The design depicting a blonde Shepard won the initial vote.<ref name="Blonde Wins"/> BioWare then held a second vote to select the design's hair colour.<ref name="Round 2"/><ref name="You Picked"/> A red-haired version won and became the default female Shepard used in ''Mass Effect 3''.<ref name="Red head"/>

For ''[[Mass Effect Legendary Edition]]'', BioWare unified Shepard's customization options across the trilogy and expanded the character creator with additional skin tones and hairstyles. The same character code could also be used across all three games, allowing a customized Shepard to retain a consistent appearance throughout the trilogy.<ref name="LE customisation">{{cite web |title=Gameplay Calibrations |url=https://www.ea.com/ea-play/news/gameplay-calibrations |website=Electronic Arts |date=6 April 2021 |access-date=29 September 2026}}</ref> The default female Shepard introduced for ''Mass Effect 3'' was made the default female appearance in all three games.<ref name="LE announcement">{{cite press release |title=Relive the Award-Winning Space Opera in Mass Effect Legendary Edition on May 14 |url=https://news.ea.com/press-releases/press-releases-details/2021/Relive-the-Award-Winning-Space-Opera-in-Mass-Effect-Legendary-Edition-on-May-14/ |publisher=Electronic Arts |date=February 2, 2021 |access-date=September 29, 2026}}</ref>

===Voice===
[[File:Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale at EXP Con 2011.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.1|[[Mark Meer]] ''(left)'' and [[Jennifer Hale]] ''(right)'' provided the voices for the male and female Shepard.]]

The male and female versions of Shepard were voiced by [[Mark Meer]] and [[Jennifer Hale]] respectively. Both of them had worked with BioWare many times previously.<ref name="Faces Behind"/>

Meer had first worked with BioWare during the creation of ''[[Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn]]'' and went on to voice other [[bit part]]s in their games. When he was first called in to work on ''Mass Effect'', he expected to voice more bit parts, and was "pleasantly surprised" to get the role of Shepard.<ref name="Meer Interview">{{cite web |url=http://www.pc.rpgsite.net/interviews/189-mark-meer-interview |title=Mark Meer Interview |author=Dave Ward |date=January 11, 2010 |work=RPG Site |access-date=May 13, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110904092714/http://pc.rpgsite.net/interviews/189-mark-meer-interview |archive-date=September 4, 2011 }}</ref><ref name="How Would">{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/how-would-commander-shepard-himself-play-an-rpg-5455467 |title=How Would Commander Shepard Himself Play an RPG? |author=Owen Good |date=January 23, 2010 |work=[[Kotaku]] |access-date=May 13, 2013 |archive-date=September 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150902223556/http://kotaku.com/5455467/how-would-commander-shepard-himself-play-an-rpg |url-status=live }}</ref> Caroline Livingstone gave voice direction during recording, and lead writer [[Mac Walters]] would occasionally sit in during recording sessions, allowing lines to be changed quickly.<ref name="Meer Interview"/>

Meer was initially directed to play Shepard as a restrained, professional military officer. He avoided making either the Paragon or Renegade responses sound so extreme that switching between them would make the character seem inconsistent. As the trilogy progressed and Shepard was placed under greater pressure, Meer was given more scope to vary the character's emotional delivery.<ref name="TechRadar oral history"/> Caroline Livingstone directed the recording sessions, with lead writer [[Mac Walters]] sometimes present so that dialogue could be revised during recording.<ref name="Meer Interview"/>
	
Hale approached Shepard primarily through the script rather than modelling the character on another science-fiction protagonist. Hale has said she is very invested in helping to "create" the stories of video games, though she herself is not a [[gamer]].<ref name="GR Hale Interview"/><ref name="Commanding Shepard"/> Although Hale does object to certain lines if they seem out-of-character in other works, she prefers not to mess with the words for Shepard and BioWare.<ref name="GR Hale Interview"/> That BioWare did not change the words based on gender considerations was one of Hale's favorite aspects of the series.<ref name="hale to">{{cite web | url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2013-06-26-hale-to-the-commander | date=2013-06-26 | work=[[Eurogamer]] | title=Hale to the Commander | first=Johnny | last=Cullen | access-date=2014-12-31 | archive-date=2014-12-30 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141230014654/http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2013-06-26-hale-to-the-commander | url-status=live }}</ref>

During recording for ''Mass Effect 3'', Hale worked with Livingstone and Walters using a system that supplied the current line together with preceding dialogue and contextual directions. Multiple readings of the same line could be recorded with different emotional emphases, allowing an appropriate take to be selected later.<ref name="Voicebox">{{cite magazine |last=Bissell |first=Tom |title=Voicebox 360 |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/08/15/voicebox-360 |magazine=The New Yorker |date=8 August 2011 |access-date=29 September 2026}}</ref> Hale said Shepard's military background informed the character's controlled delivery. The branching dialogue also required her to avoid carrying an emotional state from one possible conversational path into lines that could be reached through another.<ref name="Voicebox"/>

==Appearances==
{{summarize section|date=January 2026}}
Shepard serves as the [[player character]] of the main ''[[Mass Effect]]'' game trilogy. The commander is a graduate of the Systems Alliance's – the "galactic face of humanity"<ref name="SA Codex"/> – military N7 program, the highest grade of their "Interplanetary Combatives Training" that commands a great deal of respect.<ref name="SO Codex"/> Their service before joining the military and the military event that allowed them to rise to fame are both chosen by the player before the game starts, out of three options each. Also customizable is Shepard's gender, [[character class]] and physical appearance.<ref name="World Atlas"/> The player is given paraphrased [[Interactive storytelling|dialogue options]] via a radial command menu called the "dialogue wheel", which Shepard will expand on when clicked. Different choices on the dialogue wheel can grant either Paragon or Renegade points, which will over time affect their physical appearance in ''Mass Effect 2'' and ''Mass Effect 3'': a higher Renegade score will cause Shepard's scars to worsen and their eyes to start glowing red, while a higher Paragon score will cause Shepard's scars to gradually heal and fade away.

Outside of the main trilogy, Shepard has been briefly mentioned in the novels ''[[Mass Effect: Ascension]]'', ''[[Mass Effect: Retribution|Retribution]]'', and ''[[Mass Effect: Deception|Deception]]'', and has also made a brief appearance in the third issue of the comic ''Homeworlds'', with only the N7 logo on their armour being shown in-shot. ''[[Mass Effect: Redemption|Redemption]]'', taking place two years before the second game's main events, concerns how Shepard's body was retrieved by [[Liara T'Soni]] and then given to Cerberus after the character's death in ''Mass Effect 2''{{'}}s [[prologue]]. The character, however, will not be making any further appearances in any ''Mass Effect'' games now that the main trilogy is over,<ref name="Remembering"/> and BioWare have said that they do not wish the next ''Mass Effect'' protagonist to just be another soldier or "Shepard 2".<ref name="Expect More"/><ref name="4 won't"/>

===''Mass Effect''===
{{Main|Mass Effect (video game)}}
In the first game, the commander is serving under [[List of Mass Effect characters#David Anderson|Captain David Anderson]] during the [[Shakedown (testing)|shakedown run]] of the highly advanced [[turian]]/human ship ''[[Normandy (Mass Effect)|SSV Normandy SR-1]]'', heading toward humanity's first ever colony, Eden Prime. However, it turns out the ship is actually being sent to collect a Prothean beacon (the Protheans being an advanced and now-extinct race whose technology could contain great discoveries) and give it to the Citadel Council, an executive committee who hold great sway in the galaxy,<ref name="Council Codex"/> and who are recognised as an authority by most of explored space.<ref name="CS Codex"/> A Spectre, an elite agent of the Council with the authority to deal with situations "in whatever way they deem necessary",<ref name="Spectres Codex"/> named Nihlus Kryik accompanies the mission to observe Shepard's candidacy to join the Spectres; if successful, this would make Shepard the first ever human Spectre and an exemplar of humanity's progress in galactic politics. However, Nihlus is killed during the mission when the [[Legion (Mass Effect)|geth]], a race of sentient AIs, and [[Saren Arterius]], a rogue Spectre, attack the colony to steal the beacon. Shepard manages to stop the colony from being destroyed but is hit by a blast from the damaged beacon before it blows up; as a result, Shepard begins to have visions of war and death.

After Saren's treachery is exposed to the Council through the use of an audio recording that mentions "the Reapers", which are believed to be a race of synthetic-organic starships that eradicate all organic civilization every 50,000 years, the Council revoke Saren's Spectre status and make Shepard the first ever human Spectre, though they believe the Reapers are merely a myth Saren is using to manipulate the geth. Shepard is instructed to take down Saren and is placed in charge of the ''Normandy'' and given free rein of the galaxy. Over the course of the game, it becomes clear that the visions are images of the Protheans being destroyed by the Reapers; the commander speaks to one of these Reapers, referred to as Sovereign, on the planet of Virmire, though the Council still believes them to be a myth.

Eventually, Saren, Sovereign and the geth launch an attack on the Citadel, the "political, cultural, and financial capital of the galactic community" and home of the Council,<ref name="Citadel Codex"/> intending to activate a mass relay inside it that will allow all the Reapers to arrive at once from dark space, destroy the Citadel, and begin their "harvest" of organic life. Shepard manages to stop them, destroy Sovereign, and save the Citadel. Depending on the player's choices, Shepard may either also save the Council, or leave them to die to ensure Sovereign is destroyed or to build a new human-centric Council.

===''Mass Effect 2''===
{{Main|Mass Effect 2}}
At the beginning of the game, Shepard is killed when the Collectors attack and destroy the ''Normandy''. The commander is revived by Cerberus, a human-supremacist organization considered to be terrorists by the Citadel Council and the Systems Alliance,<ref name="TIM Codex"/> with instructions by Cerberus leader the [[Illusive Man]] to be brought back unaltered and exactly as they were before their death. The Illusive Man provides Shepard with both a new ship (the ''Normandy SR-2'') and a crew, and sends them on various missions against the Collectors, who are revealed to be puppets of the Reapers.

Over the course of the game, Shepard must assemble a team to prepare for a final assault on the Collector base accessible only through the Omega-4 Relay, a relay that destroys all non-Collector ships that try to go through it. Depending on the player's choices during the final mission, it is possible that Shepard may fail to escape the Collector base and die, though the save cannot be imported to ''Mass Effect 3'' if this is the case.<ref name="May Not Work"/> At the end of this mission, the player is given the choice to either destroy the base or hand it over to Cerberus – if the player chooses the former, Shepard effectively cuts all ties with Cerberus, and the crew and squadmates join the commander.

Depending on the player's decision concerning the Council in the first game, Shepard can either be reinstated as a Spectre now that they have been revived, be rejected by Udina and the rest of the Council or refuse Spectre status when offered it.

===''Mass Effect 3''===
{{Main|Mass Effect 3}}
Shepard has been grounded and stripped of rank by the Alliance before the game starts, due to either working with Cerberus or blowing up a Mass Relay in the ''Mass Effect 2'' DLC pack ''[[Mass Effect 2: Arrival|Arrival]]''. After Earth is invaded by the Reapers, the Alliance reinstates them and sends them to ask the Council for help, retaking command of the Alliance-refitted ''Normandy SR-2''. Though the Council refuses, they either reinstate or uphold the commander's Spectre status.

Shepard must then work to forge alliances between the various alien races to ensure the survival of Earth, to fight against Cerberus forces from disrupting the war efforts, and to stop the Reapers from eradicating all organic life from the galaxy. Among the major decisions made by the player as part of the branching narrative of ''Mass Effect 3'' include the resolution of the [[Krogan|Krogan Genophage storyline]], the outcome of the war between the geth and the [[quarian]]s, and ultimately the fate of the Reapers and the rest of the galactic community.

Following the conclusion of one of the three original endings of ''Mass Effect 3'', where Shepard activates a superweapon known as the Crucible on the Citadel to deal with the Reapers, the ''Normandy'' crashes on a distant planet after being caught in a wave of energy emitted by the Crucible. In some of the possible ending scenarios, the crew eulogizes Shepard by putting his or her name on the ship's memorial and flying away. If Shepard chose to destroy the Reapers with certain requirements fulfilled, however, the crew will hesitate placing Shepard's name on the memorial wall. In one possible ending, the chestpiece of a body with the N7 emblem is shown to be moving, suggesting Shepard might have survived.

===''Mass Effect: Andromeda''===
{{Main|Mass Effect: Andromeda}}
Shepard does not make a direct appearance, though players can select Shepard's gender at the start of the game. Shepard is referenced both in conversations between characters, and in audio logs sent by Liara T'Soni to Alec Ryder, the player character's father.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/mass-effect-andromeda/mass-effect-andromeda-shepard |title=You can choose Shepard's - yes, Shepard's - gender in Mass Effect: Andromeda |date=February 23, 2017 |work=PCGamesN |access-date=February 23, 2017 |archive-date=June 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220627214147/https://www.pcgamesn.com/mass-effect-andromeda/mass-effect-andromeda-shepard |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Promotion and merchandise==
The default male Shepard was used heavily in marketing, being featured on the covers for all three games and most trailers. The female Shepard was confirmed to be making an appearance in one of the trailers for the third game, and on one side of '' Mass Effect 3''{{'}}s Collector's Edition, in June 2011.<ref name="To Appear"/> The female Shepard had not been advertised heavily previously as marketing wanted to only showcase one character, so that consumers could easily understand who the hero was. For ''Mass Effect 3'', BioWare wished to "acknowledge" the demand for material with the female Shepard.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vg247.com/2011/07/19/loving-femshep-biowares-first-lady-finally-steps-forward/ |title=Loving FemShep: BioWare's first lady finally steps forward |author=Brenna Hillier |date=July 19, 2011 |work=VG247 |access-date=May 12, 2013 |archive-date=April 29, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130429121223/http://www.vg247.com/2011/07/19/loving-femshep-biowares-first-lady-finally-steps-forward/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Outside of the ''Mass Effect'' series, Shepard has also made cameo appearances in other [[Electronic Arts]] games. ''SkyHeroes'' features various different characters from EA games, acting as playable pilots during the game's multiplayer mode.<ref name="So Cute"/> Through [[downloadable content]] released on March 27, Shepard becomes available as an alternate skin for Serah and Noel within ''Final Fantasy XIII-2''.<ref name="Fantasy Costume"/><ref name="Shepard Approved"/> An N7 armor and omni-blades become available in ''[[Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning]]'' if the demo for ''[[Mass Effect 3]]'' has been completed;<ref name="Meets KoA"/> similarly, an N7 armor becomes available in ''[[Dead Space 3]]'' if the player owns a copy of ''Mass Effect 3''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.digitalspy.co.uk/gaming/news/a452789/dead-space-3-to-receive-bonus-mass-effect-3-themed-armour.html |title='Dead Space 3' to receive bonus 'Mass Effect 3' themed armour |author=Matthew Reynolds |date=January 22, 2013 |work=[[Digital Spy]] |access-date=May 9, 2013 |archive-date=May 16, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130516095111/http://www.digitalspy.co.uk/gaming/news/a452789/dead-space-3-to-receive-bonus-mass-effect-3-themed-armour.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.technologytell.com/gaming/106101/mass-effect-n7-armor-comes-to-dead-space-3/ |title=Mass Effect N7 armor comes to Dead Space 3 |author=Jeremy Hill |date=January 21, 2013 |work=Gamertell |access-date=May 9, 2013 |archive-date=April 1, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130401114104/http://www.technologytell.com/gaming/106101/mass-effect-n7-armor-comes-to-dead-space-3/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Reception==
Commander Shepard has received a generally positive reception and often appeared in reader's polls published by video game publications.<ref name="GI Readers'"/><ref name="Poll1">{{cite web |url= https://www.ign.com/star-wars-knights-of-the-old-republic/85193/feature/the-ultimate-rpg-party-revealed|title=THE ULTIMATE RPG PARTY REVEALED|date=December 17, 2014 |work=IGN |access-date=March 19, 2020 |url-status= dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141217231416/https://www.ign.com/articles/2014/12/17/the-ultimate-rpg-party |archive-date=December 17, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Poll2">{{cite web|url=http://www.pcgamer.com/ranking-the-best-and-worst-of-the-mass-effect-games/|title=Ranking the best and worst of the Mass Effect games|author=Tyler Wilde|date=August 7, 2015|access-date=March 18, 2020|publisher=[[PC Gamer]]|archive-date=August 11, 2015|archive-url=https://archive.today/20150811200917/http://www.pcgamer.com/ranking-the-best-and-worst-of-the-mass-effect-games/|url-status=live}}</ref> Shepard was voted the primary [[Xbox 360]] candidate in ''[[IGN]]''{{'}}s mock video game presidential election.<ref name="Xbox Primary"/><ref name="IGN Winners"/>

Shepard has appeared in numerous top video game character lists compiled by video game publications.<ref name="8 Coolest"/> [[GameDaily]],<ref name="Hunks"/><ref name="100 Best"/> Joe Juba, writing for ''Game Informer'', chose Shepard as their favourite protagonist in their "2012 RPG of the Year Awards", saying that while the player changed the tone and context of many parts of ''Mass Effect'', "Shepard never comes out of it looking any less awesome".<ref name="GI Awards"/>

Not all critical reception has been positive. ''[[Maxim (magazine)|Maxim]]'' described the visual design of Shepard's armor as derivative.<ref name="Power Suits"/> Andrew Goldfarb, for ''[[IGN]]'', criticized the decision to revisit Shepard during the [[downloadable content]] of ''[[Mass Effect 3]]'', believing that ''3''{{'}}s ending was "final", and saying that he would have preferred to have a look at a new squad separate from Shepard.<ref name="Doesn't Need"/>

===Female Shepard===
Although female Shepard is less popular with players compared to her male counterpart, the character and her voice actress has consistently been well received critically.<ref name="15 Things">{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamer.com/2011/02/16/15-things-we-want-to-see-in-mass-effect-3/ |title=15 things we want to see in Mass Effect 3 |last=Francis |first=Tom |date=February 16, 2011 |work=[[PC Gamer]] |access-date=May 12, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130316093253/http://www.pcgamer.com/2011/02/16/15-things-we-want-to-see-in-mass-effect-3/ |archive-date=March 16, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Hale was nominated for "Best Performance By A Human Female" at the 2010 [[Spike Video Game Awards]],<ref name="Spike Nominees"/> though lost to fellow ''Mass Effect'' voice actor [[Tricia Helfer]] (playing [[Sarah Kerrigan]] in ''[[StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty]]'').<ref name="Spike Winners"/> 
''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]'' included Jane Shepard, the default name for a female Shepard, in their list of the 70 best video game characters of the 2010s decade, with Cass Marshall singling out Hale's voice acting for convincingly selling her character as "both a deadly space marine and a vulnerable protagonist facing impossible odds".<ref name=Decade>{{Cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/features/2019/11/27/20974490/greatest-video-game-characters-2019-2010-skyrim-witcher-splatoon|title=The 70 best video game characters of the decade|first=Polygon|last=Staff|website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|date=November 27, 2019|access-date=June 11, 2023|archive-date=November 27, Various media outlets like [[CNET]], ''ONE37pm'' and ''[[Comic Book Resources|CBR]]'' have included Commander Shepard in their lists of top female video game characters.<ref>{{Cite The outcome of the design poll, which was initially won by the blonde Shepard, was described as controversial and proved divisive with critics. While commentators like Kirk Hamilton from ''Kotaku'' accepted what he perceived to be a legitimately democratic choice, others like Kim Richards from ''PC Gamer'' rejected the outcome.<ref name="Blonde Wins"/><ref name="Blonde1">{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/fans-picked-the-blonde-in-a-controversial-video-game-be-5826702|title=Fans Picked the Blonde in a Controversial Video Game Beauty Contest, But That's Not a Bad Thing|author=Kirk Hamilton|date=August 1, 2011|website=[[Kotaku]]|access-date=May 16, 2021|archive-date=May 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517081920/https://kotaku.com/fans-picked-the-blonde-in-a-controversial-video-game-be-5826702|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Blonde2">{{cite web|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/mass-effect-3-death-to-blonde-shepard/|title=Mass Effect 3: Death to Blonde Shepard|author=Kim Richards|date=July 27, 2011|access-date=March 16, 2020|work=[[PC Gamer]]|archive-date=September 5, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220905223549/https://www.pcgamer.com/mass-effect-3-death-to-blonde-shepard/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Blonde3">{{cite web|url=https://www.destructoid.com/stories/why-the-mass-effect-3-femshep-vote-was-the-wrong-move-208186.phtml|title=Why the Mass Effect 3 FemShep vote was the wrong move|author=Sophie Prell|date=August 12, 2011|access-date=May 19, 2021|work=[[Destructoid]]|archive-date=February 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202225953/https://www.destructoid.com/stories/why-the-mass-effect-3-femshep-vote-was-the-wrong-move-208186.phtml|url-status=live}}</ref> Richards in particular criticized the poll for encouraging players to go for the most "[[Barbie]]-like" conventionally attractive appearance.<ref name="Blonde2"/>

Carlen Lavigne's later analysis of the controversy concluded that the poll was presented like a beauty contest, which positioned Shepard in a sexualized manner for the pleasure of a [[male gaze|straight male audience]]; this has a corrupting effect on Shepard's standing as a feminist lead, even though the original intention is to promote a female character as the face of the franchise.<ref name="Future">{{cite journal |last=Lavigne |first=Carlen |title='She's a soldier, not a model': Feminism, FemShep and the Mass Effect 3 vote|date=September 1, 2015|volume= 7| number =3 |journal= Journal of Gaming & Virtual Worlds}}</ref> The authors of ''Bridging Game Studies and Feminist Theories'' noted that the poll produced "six avatars who have the exact same body shape, but are distinguished by different skin, hair, and eye colour." From their point of view, Shepard would either way "fit perfectly with beauty standards while creating the illusion of choice for players."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.kinephanos.ca/2017/bridging-game-studies-and-feminist-theories/ | title=Bridging Game Studies and Feminist Theories | Kinephanos | access-date=2023-06-19 | archive-date=2023-05-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230527103947/https://www.kinephanos.ca/2017/bridging-game-studies-and-feminist-theories/ | url-status=live }}</ref> Leandro Lima noted that the manner in which Shepard was included within the marketing campaign for ''Mass Effect 3'' was still problematic for many players, as she is "perceived as very generic in terms of design".<ref name="Configurative">{{cite journal |last=Lima |first=Leandro |title="It's [not just] in the game": the promotional context of video games|at=Configurative Dynamics of Gender in Bioware's Marketing for the Mass Effect Franchise|date=November 2017|volume= 7| number =3 |journal= Kinephanos: Journal of Media Studies and Popular Culture}}</ref> Patricia Hernandez from ''Polygon'' felt that the manner which the female Shepard poll unfolded was "strange" and that BioWare's attempts to continue modifying her years after the release of the first game while her male counterpart's appearance remains unchanged is somewhat "off-putting". Nevertheless, she expressed relief that "in 2021, there's no vote, no massive fan campaign to get BioWare to even ''consider'' highlighting FemShep" in response to the character's prominence in promotional material released for ''Mass Effect Legendary Edition''.<ref name="polygon femshep">{{cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/2021/2/3/22264224/mass-effect-remastered-femshep-legendary-edition-jennifer-hale-bioware|title=Mass Effect's decadelong FemShep saga finally comes to a close|first=Patricia|last=Hernandez|website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|date=3 February 2021|access-date=May 19, 2021|archive-date=5 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220905223547/https://www.polygon.com/2021/2/3/22264224/mass-effect-remastered-femshep-legendary-edition-jennifer-hale-bioware|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Della Duck]] (twin sister)

[[Gladstone Gander]] (cousin) | nationality = American }} '''Donald Fauntleroy Duck''' is a cartoon character created by [[Walt Disney]] and [[Dick Lundy (animator)|Dick Lundy]]. Donald is an [[Anthropomorphism|anthropomorphic]] white [[duck]] with a yellow-orange bill, legs, and feet. He typically wears a [[sailor suit|sailor shirt and cap]] with a [[bow tie]]. Often described by critics and scholars as a global pop culture icon of animation, Donald is known for his [[Donald Duck talk|semi-intelligible speech]] and his volatile, boisterous, and high-energy personality. Along with his friend and rival [[Mickey Mouse]], Donald is one of the most recognizable characters owned by [[the Walt Disney Company]], and was included in ''[[TV Guide]]''{{'}}s list of the 50 greatest cartoon characters of all time in 2002,{{cite web|url=http://articles.cnn.com/2002-07-30/entertainment/cartoon.characters.list_1_ren-and-stimpy-tv-guide-space-ghost|title=TV Guide's 50 greatest cartoon characters of all time|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716085538/http://articles.cnn.com/2002-07-30/entertainment/cartoon.characters.list_1_ren-and-stimpy-tv-guide-space-ghost|archive-date=July 16, 2011|website=[[CNN]]|date=June 30, 2002|access-date=June 4, 2011}} as well as earning a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]]. He is Disney's most prolific cartoon character.Not including television episodes but including short films, Donald has appeared in 197 films. ([https://web.archive.org/web/20170725075622/https://www.imdb.com/character/ch0000719/ Donald Duck] at IMDb, retrieved August 15, 2014) The Disney character with the second most film appearances is Mickey Mouse at 167. ([https://web.archive.org/web/20170725075827/http://www.imdb.com/character/ch0000630/ Mickey Mouse] at IMDb, retrieved August 15, 2014) Donald Duck has appeared in over 150 animated short films in the [[golden age of American animation]], several of which were recognized at the [[Academy Awards]]. Donald's first appearance was in the ''[[Silly Symphony]]'' film ''[[The Wise Little Hen]]'' (1934), but was reworked as a temperamental comic [[Foil (narrative)|foil]] to Mickey Mouse in ''[[Orphan's Benefit]]''.{{cite book|last=Maltin|first=Leonard|author-link=Leonard Maltin|title=Of Mice and Magic: A History of American Animated Cartoons|date=1987|page=49|edition=Revised|publisher=Plume|isbn=0-452-25993-2}} In the 1930s, he typically appeared as part of a comic trio with Mickey and [[Goofy]] and was given his own film series starting with ''[[Don Donald]]'' (1937). These films introduced Donald's love interest and permanent girlfriend [[Daisy Duck]] and often included his three nephews [[Huey, Dewey, and Louie]]. Donald gradually outshone Mickey, who was relegated to a side character in newer cartoons while Donald maintained his own series until 1961. After the film ''[[Chips Ahoy (film)|Chips Ahoy]]'' (1956), Donald appeared primarily in educational films before eventually returning to theatrical animation in ''[[Mickey's Christmas Carol]]'' (1983). His final appearance in a theatrical film was in ''[[Fantasia 2000]]'' (1999). However, since then Donald has appeared in direct-to-video features such as ''[[Mickey, Donald, Goofy: The Three Musketeers]]'' (2004), television series such as ''[[Mickey Mouse Clubhouse]]'' (2006–2016), and video games such as ''[[QuackShot]]'' (1991), ''[[Donald Duck: Goin' Quackers]]'' (2000) and the ''[[Kingdom Hearts]]'' series (2002–present). In addition to animation, Donald is well known worldwide for his [[Donald Duck in comics|appearances in comics]]. Donald was most famously drawn by [[Al Taliaferro]], [[Carl Barks]], and [[Don Rosa]]. Barks, in particular, is credited for greatly expanding the "[[Donald Duck universe]]", the world in which Donald lives, and creating many additional characters such as Donald's rich uncle [[Scrooge McDuck]]. Donald has been a popular character in Europe, particularly in [[Nordic countries]]. In [[Italy]], Donald is a major character in many [[Disney comics#Italy|comics]], including a juvenile version named Paperino Paperotto, and a superhero alter ego known as ''[[Paperinik]]'' (''Duck Avenger'' in the US and ''[[Super Duck|Super duck]]'' in the UK). ==Characteristics== ===Appearance=== Donald Duck is portrayed as a white duck with a yellow-orange bill, legs, and webbed feet, the color pattern of a domestic duck of the [[American Pekin]] breed,{{cite web |title=Pekin Ducks |url=https://breeds.okstate.edu/poultry/ducks/pekin-ducks.html |access-date=27 June 2023 |website=Oklahoma State University Extension – Department of Food & Animal Sciences |date=20 July 2021 }} but instead of wings he has arms and three-fingered hands with opposable thumbs. He usually wears an originally black, later blue sailor shirt with white or yellow accents, a black or red bow tie, and a blue sailor's cap, but no pants or footwear. ===Voice=== {{Main|Donald Duck talk}} {{Listen|filename=Voice of Donald Duck in Modern Inventions.ogg|title=Donald's voice|description=Donald's voice in ''[[Modern Inventions]]'' (1937)}} The character is known for possessing an only partly intelligible voice, developed by Donald's original performer, [[Clarence Nash]]. During an interview, Tony Anselmo revealed that "Most people believe that Donald's voice is done squeezing air through the cheek, that is not true. I can't reveal how it's actually done, but it is definitely not done by squeezing air through the cheek. The [[Hanna-Barbera]] character '[[Yakky Doodle]]' is done that way. Donald Duck is not."{{cite web|url=https://www.latestly.com/entertainment/hollywood/uncovering-donald-ducks-official-voice-tony-anselmo-3304518.html|title=Uncovering Donald Duck's Official Voice|date=Jan 29, 2022|access-date=April 27, 2022|archive-date=May 19, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220519143805/https://www.latestly.com/entertainment/hollywood/uncovering-donald-ducks-official-voice-tony-anselmo-3304518.html|url-status=live}} Nash reputedly originally developed the voice as that of a "nervous baby goat" before Walt Disney interpreted it as sounding like a duck.{{cite book|last=Blitz|first=Marcia|title=Donald Duck|year=1979|page=19|publisher=[[Harmony Books]]|location=[[New York City|New York]]|isbn=978-0-517-52961-4}} ===Personality=== [[File:Donald Duck - temper.png|thumb|Donald Duck is known for his fiery temper.]] Donald Duck is portrayed as an impatient, immature,{{cite web|url=https://www.looper.com/278078/the-untold-truth-of-donald-duck/|title=The Untold Truth of Donald Duck|date=November 12, 2020|access-date=June 2, 2022|archive-date=May 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220529105803/https://www.looper.com/278078/the-untold-truth-of-donald-duck/|url-status=live}} and arrogant duck with a pessimistic attitude and an insecure disposition. In addition, his two dominant personality traits are his fiery temper and his cynical attitude to life. Donald typically starts off every cartoon in a jolly mood until certain events happen to anger him, in part due to his antagonistic behavior, jealousy or general incompetence. His rage proves to be disadvantageous when he goes too far, though he is capable of temporarily controlling his temper, if not enough to handle his conflicts. However, he is capable of courage and perseverance, able to defeat threats of any kind and complete difficult tasks when combined with his outbursts. Donald has a [[Mischief|mischievous]] side, taking delight in causing chaos as well as imposing superiority on [[Chip n' Dale|Chip and Dale]] and [[Huey, Dewey and Louie]]. As animator [[Fred Spencer]] put it: {{blockquote|The Duck gets a big kick out of imposing on other people or annoying them, but he immediately loses his temper when the tables are turned. In other words, he can dish it out, but he can't take it.Walt Disney Treasures: The Chronological Donald Volume One}} However, with a few exceptions, Donald means no ill will and is apologetic at times. In ''[[Truant Officer Donald]]'', for example, when he is tricked into believing he has accidentally killed Huey, Dewey, and Louie, he shows great regret, blaming himself. His nephews appear in the form of angels, and he willingly endures a kick by one of them—that is, of course, until he realizes he has been tricked, whereupon he promptly loses his temper. Donald is also a bit of a [[poseur]]. As a jack of all trades, he typically overestimates his abilities out of [[hubris]], so that when he sets out to make good on his boasts, he fails spectacularly to hilarious effect. A [[running gag]] in the Donald Duck comics involves him being physically unhealthy and unmotivated to [[exercise]] in spite of his appearance and achievements. Donald had a stint in the [[U.S. Army]] during [[World War II]] that culminated with him serving as a commando in the film ''[[Commando Duck]]'', and he was frequently away serving in the [[U.S. Navy]] in the television cartoon series ''[[DuckTales (1987 TV series)|DuckTales]]''. ===Friendly rivalry with Mickey Mouse=== Donald is occasionally shown as a [[Foil (narrative)|foil]] of [[Mickey Mouse]], being envious of his success and refusing to be [[second banana]], in spite of his popularity surpassing that of Mickey's in real life. [[Chuck Jones]] used this relationship as the basis for the rivalry between [[Daffy Duck]] and [[Bugs Bunny]] in his cartoons. In most Disney theatrical cartoons, Mickey and Donald are shown as friends and have little to no rivalry (exceptions being ''[[The Band Concert]],'' ''[[Magician Mickey]]'' and near the end of ''[[Symphony Hour]], ''which were due to Donald's antagonistic schemes). However, by the time ''[[The Mickey Mouse Club]]'' aired on television, it was shown that Donald always wanted the spotlight. In the TV special ''[[Mickey's 60th Birthday]]'', Mickey is cursed by a [[Magician (fantasy)|sorcerer]] to become unnoticed, causing Donald Duck to be arrested for the apparent [[kidnapping]] of Mickey, but his charges are dismissed due to a lack of evidence. [[Walt Disney]], in his ''[[Walt Disney anthology television series#Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color (1961–1969)|Wonderful World of Color]]'', would sometimes make reference to the rivalry. Walt, one time, had presented Donald with a gigantic [[birthday cake]] and commented how it was "even bigger than Mickey's", which pleased Donald. The clip was rebroadcast in November 1984 during a [[Donald Duck's 50th Birthday|TV special]] honoring Donald's 50th birthday, with [[Dick Van Dyke]] substituting for Walt. The rivalry between Mickey and Donald was shown in the 2001-2003 television series ''[[House of Mouse]]''. It was shown that Donald wanted to be the club's founder and wanted to change the name from ''House of Mouse'' to ''House of Duck'', which is obvious in the episodes "The Stolen Cartoons" and "Timon and Pumbaa". In the episode "Everybody Loves Mickey", Donald's jealousy is explored and even joins sides with Mortimer Mouse. However, Donald has a change of heart when Daisy reminds Donald how Mickey has always been there to support him. Since then, Donald accepted that Mickey was the founder and worked with Mickey as a partner to make the club profitable and successful. ===Enemies=== Donald has numerous enemies, who range from comical foil to nemesis: [[Chip 'n' Dale]], [[Pete (Disney)|Pete]], [[Humphrey the Bear]], Spike the Bee, Mountain Lion Louie, Bootle Beetle, [[Witch Hazel (Disney)|Witch Hazel]] (in ''Trick or Treat''), [[Aracuan Bird]] and Baby Shelby (in ''[[Mickey Mouse Works]]''). During the [[Second World War]], [[propaganda]] cartoons produced saw Donald set against [[Adolf Hitler]] and [[Nazi Germany]].{{cite book|last=Hake|first=Sabine|title=Screen Nazis: Cinema, History, and Democracy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Lu4R9wQouSYC&pg=PA38|date=August 31, 2012|page=38|publisher=University of Wisconsin Pres|isbn=978-0-299-28713-9}} In the comics, he is often harassed or on the run from the [[Beagle Boys]], [[Magica De Spell]], [[Gladstone Gander]] and [[List of Donald Duck characters#Neighbor Jones|Mr. Jones]]. ==Origin== Voice performer [[Clarence Nash]] auditioned for [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Productions]] when he learned that Disney was looking for people to create animal sounds for his cartoons. Disney was particularly impressed with Nash's duck imitation and chose him to voice the new character. Disney came up with Donald's iconic attributes including his short temper and his sailor suit (based on ducks and sailors both being associated with water).{{harv|Andrae|2006|p=61}} While [[Dick Huemer]] and [[Art Babbit]] were the first to animate Donald, [[Dick Lundy (animator)|Dick Lundy]] is credited for developing him as a character.{{sfn|Watts|2013|p=253}} On April 29, 1934, five days before ''[[The Wise Little Hen]]'s'' first theatrical release, bandleader Raymond Paige performed the score to the cartoon on his ''California Melodies'' program for the Los Angeles AM radio station [[KHJ (AM)|KHJ]]. The main vocals were performed by a trio, the Three Rhythm Kings. Clarence Nash and [[Florence Gill]] performed the character voices for this radio treatment, with Nash performing both Donald Duck and Peter Pig, making it the first time the public heard Nash's duck voice.{{cite web|last=Kaufman|first=J.B.|author-link=J.B. Kaufman|title=When's Your Birthday?|url=https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/whens-your-birthday/|website=[[Jerry Beck|Cartoon Research]]|access-date=September 26, 2020|date=June 8, 2020|archive-date=October 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201001185624/https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/whens-your-birthday/|url-status=live}} An apocryphal alternative story for how Donald was created came about from a claim that Disney was watching an exhibition [[cricket]] match between [[Australia cricket team|Australia]] and the New York [[West Indies cricket team|West Indians]] and Australia's star batsman [[Don Bradman]] was [[Dismissal (cricket)|out]] for a [[duck (cricket)|duck]]. Disney allegedly used this as inspiration for the character. However, the veracity of this has been doubted by modern historians.{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/articles/cqqq27rxlz5o|title=T20 World Cup: Cricket in USA awaits Disney's authentic Donald Duck moment|date=June 2024|access-date=June 1, 2024|archive-date=June 1, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601132723/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/articles/cqqq27rxlz5o|url-status=live}} ==Animation== ===Early development=== {{further|Donald Duck filmography}} [[File:Donald duck debut.PNG|thumb|Donald Duck as he first appeared in ''[[The Wise Little Hen]]'' (1934)]] Donald Duck's first film appearance was in the 1934 cartoon ''[[The Wise Little Hen]]'', which was part of the ''[[Silly Symphonies]]'' series of theatrical cartoon shorts.{{cite book|last=Finch|first=Christopher|title=The Art of Walt Disney: From Mickey Mouse to the Magic Kingdoms|url=https://archive.org/details/artofwaltdisneyf00finc/page/40/mode/2up|date=1988|page=40|publisher=Twin Books|isbn=0-517-66474-7|access-date=9 October 2020}} The film's given release date of June 9 is officially recognized by the Walt Disney Company as Donald's birthday,{{cite web|title=When is Donald Duck's birthday? When did he debut?|work=Guest Services|publisher=Disney|url=http://home.disney.go.com/guestservices/faqs#history_archives8|access-date=June 7, 2016|archive-date=September 1, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070901031224/http://home.disney.go.com/guestservices/faqs#history_archives8|url-status=dead}} though historian [[J.B. Kaufman]], consultant of the [[Walt Disney Family Museum]], discovered in recent years that ''The Wise Little Hen'' was first shown on May 3, 1934, at the [[Carthay Circle Theater]] for a [[Benefit performance|benefit program]], while its official debut was on June 7 at the [[Radio City Music Hall]]. Donald's appearance in the cartoon, as created by animator [[Dick Lundy (animator)|Dick Lundy]], is similar to his modern look – the feather and beak colors are the same, as are the blue sailor shirt and hat – but his features are more elongated, his body plumper, his feet smaller, and his sclerae white. Donald's personality is not developed in the short, being presented as a generic anthropomorphic duck. [[Peter Pig]] was also introduced in the film, but never caught on as a character due to his overt resemblance to [[Porky Pig]]. [[Burt Gillett]] brought Donald back in a 1934 [[Mickey Mouse]] cartoon, ''[[Orphans' Benefit]]''. Donald is one of a number of characters who are giving performances in a benefit for Mickey's Orphans.{{sfn|Watts|2013|p=252}} Donald's act is to recite the poems "[[Mary Had a Little Lamb]]" and "[[Little Boy Blue]]", but every time he tries, the mischievous orphans heckle him, leading the duck to fly into a squawking fit of anger. This explosive personality would remain with Donald for decades to come. Donald continued to be a hit with audiences. The character began appearing regularly in most Mickey Mouse cartoons. Cartoons from this period, such as the cartoon ''[[The Band Concert]]'' (1935) – in which Donald repeatedly disrupts the Mickey Mouse Orchestra's rendition of [[The William Tell Overture|''The William Tell'' Overture]] by playing "[[Turkey in the Straw]]" – are regularly noted by critics as exemplary films and classics of animation. Animator [[Ben Sharpsteen]] also created the classic Mickey, Donald, and Goofy comedy formula in 1935, with the cartoon ''Mickey's Service Station''.{{sfn|Watts|2013|p=252}} In 1936, Donald was redesigned to be a bit fuller, rounder, and cuter, beginning with the cartoon ''[[Moving Day (1936 film)|Moving Day]]''. He also began starring in solo cartoons, the first of which was Ben Sharpsteen's 1937 cartoon, ''[[Don Donald]]''. This short also introduced a love interest of Donald's, ''Donna Duck'', who evolved into [[Daisy Duck]].Although the Walt Disney Company claimed Donna Duck to be the same character as Donald's longtime love interest [[Daisy Duck]], this is not so in Karp/Taliaferro comics (1951), where she is a separate character, appearing together with Daisy in a couple of daily newspaper strips. Early illustrations of Daisy also show a clear distinction between the two, Donna having a Mexican accent, contrary to Daisy. Donald's nephews, [[Huey, Dewey and Louie]], would make their first animated appearance a year later in the 1938 film, ''[[Donald's Nephews]]'', directed by [[Jack King (animator)|Jack King]] (they had been earlier introduced in the [[Donald Duck (comic strip)|''Donald Duck'' comic strip]] by [[Al Taliaferro]], see below). By 1938, most polls showed that Donald was more popular than Mickey Mouse.{{cite web|url=http://www.bcdb.com/bcdb/cartoon.cgi?film=15&m=r|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120529015403/http://www.bcdb.com/bcdb/cartoon.cgi?film=15&m=r|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 29, 2012|title=Free Cartoon Reviews of Fantasia Feature Length Theatrical Animated Film|publisher=Bcdb.com|access-date=August 1, 2011}} ===Wartime=== [[File:Ducknazi.jpg|thumb|left|Donald worked in a Nazi factory during a nightmare in ''[[Der Fuehrer's Face]]'' (1943).]] During [[World War II]], Donald appeared in several animated [[propaganda film|propaganda films]], including the 1943 ''[[Der Fuehrer's Face]]''. In this cartoon, Donald plays a worker in an artillery factory in "Nutzi Land" ([[Nazi Germany]]). He struggles with long working hours, very small food rations,{{cite web|title=Donald Duck does it in style|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/3790213.stm|work=[[BBC News]]|date=June 9, 2004|access-date=October 4, 2012}} and having to [[Nazi salute|salute]] every time he sees a picture of the [[Führer]] ([[Adolf Hitler]]). These pictures appear in many places, such as on the assembly line in which he is screwing in the detonators of various sizes of shells. In the end, he becomes little more than a small part in a faceless machine with no choice but to obey until he falls, suffering a nervous breakdown. Then Donald wakes up to find that his experience was, in fact, a dream. At the end of the short, Donald looks to the [[Statue of Liberty]] and the American flag with renewed appreciation. ''Der Fuehrer's Face'' won the 1942 [[Academy Award for Animated Short Film]]. ''Der Fuehrer's Face'' was also the first of two animated short films to be set during the War to win an Oscar, the other being the ''[[Tom and Jerry]]'' short film ''[[The Yankee Doodle Mouse]]''.{{sfn|Watts|2013|pages=230–231}} Other shorts from this period include a six film mini-series that follows Donald's life in the [[U.S. Army]] from his drafting to his experiences in basic training under Sergeant [[Pete (Disney)|Pete]] to his first actual mission as a [[commando]] having to sabotage a Japanese air base. Titles in the series include: {{clear left}} *''[[Donald Gets Drafted]]'' (May 1, 1942){{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/disney/10885903/Donald-Duck-10-surprising-facts-about-Walt-Disneys-character.html|archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220111/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/disney/10885903/Donald-Duck-10-surprising-facts-about-Walt-Disneys-character.html|archive-date=January 11, 2022|url-access=subscription|url-status=live|title=Donald Duck: 10 surprising facts about Walt Disney's character|journal=The Daily Telegraph|date=June 9, 2014|access-date=November 8, 2017|language=en-GB|issn=0307-1235}}{{cbignore}} *''[[The Vanishing Private]]'' (September 25, 1942) *''[[Sky Trooper]]'' (November 8, 1942) *''[[Fall Out Fall In]]'' (April 23, 1943) *''[[The Old Army Game]]'' (November 5, 1943) *''[[Commando Duck]]'' (June 2, 1944) Thanks in part to these films, Donald graced the [[nose art]]work of virtually every type of World War II [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] combat aircraft, from the [[L-4 Grasshopper]] to the [[B-29 Superfortress]].{{cite web|title=Military Aircraft Nose Art|url=http://www.nasflmuseum.com/nose-art.html|publisher=Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale Museum|access-date=October 4, 2012|archive-date=June 15, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120615051628/http://www.nasflmuseum.com/nose-art.html|url-status=live}} Donald also appears as a mascot—such as in the [[United States Army Air Forces]]' [[309th Fighter Squadron]]{{cite web|title=309th Fighter Squadron|publisher=31st Fighter Group|url=http://www.31stfightergroup.com/31stReference/history/309th.html|access-date=2007-08-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070823135236/http://www.31stfightergroup.com/31stReference/history/309th.html |archive-date=August 23, 2007}} and the [[U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary]], which showed Donald as a fierce-looking pirate ready to defend the American coast from invaders.{{cite web|last=Noble|first=Dennis L.|title=The Corsair Fleet|work=The Beach Patrol and Corsair Fleet|publisher=Coast Guard|date=June 2001|url=http://www.uscg.mil/history/articles/BeachPatrolCorsairFleet.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212112129/http://www.uscg.mil/history/articles/BeachPatrolCorsairFleet.pdf|archive-date=February 12, 2012|url-status=dead}} Donald also appeared as a mascot emblem for the [[415th Fighter Squadron]]; [[438th Fighter Squadron]]; [[479th Bombardment Squadron]]; and [[531st Bombardment Squadron]]. He also appeared as the mascot for the [[Fire Department]] at [[Marine Corps Air Station El Toro]], as well as the Army Air Forces (now currently the [[United States Air Force]]) 319 Aircraft Maintenance Unit at [[Luke Air Force Base]] {{emdash}} where he is seen wearing an old-style pilot's uniform with a board with a nail in it in one hand, and a lightning bolt in the other hand. Donald's most famous appearance, however, was on the North American Aviation B-25B Mitchell medium bomber (S/N 40-2261) piloted by Lt. Ted W. Lawson of the 95th Bombardment Squadron, USAAF. The aircraft, named the "Ruptured Duck" and carrying a picture of Donald's face above a pair of crossed crutches, was one of sixteen B-25Bs which took off from the aircraft carrier [[USS Hornet (CV-8)|USS ''Hornet'']] to bomb Tokyo on April 18, 1942, during the [[Doolittle Raid]]. The mission was led by Lieutenant Colonel (later General) [[Jimmy Doolittle]]. Like most of the aircraft that participated in the mission, the Ruptured Duck was unable to reach its assigned landing field in China following the raid and ended up ditching off the coast near Shangchow, China. The Ruptured Duck's pilot survived, with the loss of a leg, and later wrote about the Doolittle Raid in the book, later to be the 1944 movie, ''[[Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo]]''. [[File:Donald Duck - Grupul 7 Vânătoare.jpg|thumb|Bf 109E of ''Grupul 7'' in 1942]] Other countries' air force units also used Donald as a mascot, such as the [[Royal Romanian Air Force]]'s ''[[Grupul 7 Vânătoare]]'' (7th Fighter Group). Depicted with his blue sailor shirt and sometimes wearing a [[Aviator badge#Romania|Romanian pilot badge]], Donald appeared on the fuselage of all the Group's fighters between 1941 and 1942. Some of the Group's pilots wore [[embroidered patch]]es on their flight suits featuring him as well.{{Cite book|last1=Moroșanu |first1=Teodor Liviu |last2=Melinte |first2=Dan Alexandru |year=2010 |title=Romanian Fighter Colors 1941-1945 |publisher=MMP Books |isbn=978-83-89450-90-6 |pages=109, 116, 129}} During World War II, Disney cartoons were not allowed to be imported into [[Occupied Europe]] owing to their propagandistic content. Since this lost Disney revenue, he decided to create a new audience for his films in South America. He decided to make a trip through various Latin American countries with his assistants, and use their experiences and impressions to create two feature-length animation films. The first was ''[[Saludos Amigos]]'' (1942), which consisted of four short segments, two of them with Donald Duck. In the first, he meets his parrot pal [[José Carioca]]. The second film was ''[[The Three Caballeros]]'' (1944), in which he meets his rooster friend [[Panchito Pistoles|Panchito]]. Several decades after the war, because Donald was never officially separated from service in either his animated shorts or his comic strips, as part of Donald's 50th Birthday celebrations during the 25th Annual [[Torrance, California]] [[Armed Forces Day]] Parade, the U.S. Army retired Donald Duck from active duty as a "Buck Sergeant"{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreedictionary.com/buck+sergeant|title=buck sergeant|publisher=The Free Dictionary|access-date=October 13, 2015|archive-date=November 7, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151107193634/http://www.thefreedictionary.com/buck+sergeant|url-status=live}} (i.e. "Buck Sergeant Duck").{{cite web|url=http://jimhillmedia.com/editor_in_chief1/b/jim_hill/archive/2011/05/29/looking-back-on-donald-duck-s-50th-birthday-celebration.aspx|title=Buck Sergeant Duck and other tales of Donald's 50th birthday celebration|first=Jim|last=Hill|website=jimhillmedia.com|access-date=October 12, 2015|archive-date=February 14, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180214051031/http://jimhillmedia.com/editor_in_chief1/b/jim_hill/archive/2011/05/29/looking-back-on-donald-duck-s-50th-birthday-celebration.aspx|url-status=dead}} ===Post-war=== {{More citations needed section|date=October 2026}} Many of Donald's films made after the war recast the duck as the brunt of some other character's pestering. Donald is seen repeatedly attacked, harassed, and ridiculed by his nephews, by the [[chipmunk]]s [[Chip 'n' Dale]], or by other characters such as [[Humphrey the Bear]], [[Spike the Bee]], [[Bootle Beetle]], the [[Aracuan Bird]], [[Louie the Mountain Lion]], or a colony of ants. In effect, much like [[Bugs Bunny]] cartoons from [[Warner Bros. Cartoons|Warner Bros]], the Disney artists had reversed the classic [[screwball comedy|screwball]] scenario perfected by [[Walter Lantz]] and others in which the main character is the ''instigator'' of these harassing behaviors, rather than the butt of them. The post-war Donald also starred in [[educational film]]s, such as ''[[Donald in Mathmagic Land]]'' and ''[[How to Have an Accident at Work]]'' (both 1959), and made cameos in various Disney projects, such as ''[[The Reluctant Dragon (1941 film)|The Reluctant Dragon]]'' (1941) and the ''[[Walt Disney anthology television series|Disneyland]]'' television show (1959). For this latter show, Donald's uncle [[Ludwig von Drake]] was created in 1961. Another uncle, [[Scrooge McDuck]], made his first animated appearance in 1967, after decades as a comics-only character. In ''[[Who Framed Roger Rabbit]]'' (1988), Donald has a piano duel scene with fellow cartoon duck character [[Daffy Duck]], voiced by [[Mel Blanc]], as a humorous reference to them being real life competitors. Donald has since appeared in several different television shows and (short) animated movies. He played roles in ''[[The Prince and the Pauper (1990 film)|The Prince and the Pauper]]'' (1990) and made a [[cameo appearance]] in ''[[A Goofy Movie]]'' (1995). Donald had a rather small part in the animated television series ''[[DuckTales (1987 TV series)|DuckTales]]''. There, Donald joins the U.S. Navy and leaves his nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie with their [[Scrooge McDuck|Uncle Scrooge]], who then has to take care of them. Donald's role in the overall series was fairly limited, as he only ended up appearing in a handful of episodes when home on leave. Some of the stories in the series were loosely based on the comics by [[Carl Barks]]. Donald made some cameo appearances in ''[[Bonkers (American TV series)|Bonkers]]'', before getting his own television show ''[[Quack Pack]]''. This series featured a modernized [[Duck family (Disney)|Duck family]]. Donald was no longer wearing his sailor suit and hat, but a Hawaiian shirt. Huey, Dewey, and Louie now are teenagers, with distinct clothing, voices, and personalities. Daisy Duck has lost her pink dress and bow and has a new haircut. No other family members, besides Ludwig von Drake, appear in ''Quack Pack'', and all other Duckburg citizens are humans and not dogs. Donald made a comeback as the star of the "Noah's Ark" segment of ''[[Fantasia 2000]]'' (1999), as first mate to Noah. Donald musters the animals to the Ark and attempts to control them. He tragically believes that Daisy has been lost, while she believes the same of him, but they are reunited at the end. All of this is etc to [[Edward Elgar]]'s ''[[Pomp and Circumstance]]'' Marches 1–4. In an alternate opening for the Disney film ''[[Chicken Little (2005 film)|Chicken Little]]'' (2005), Donald would have made a cameo appearance as "Ducky Lucky". This scene can be found on the ''Chicken Little'' DVD. Donald also played an important role in ''[[Mickey Mouse Works]]'' and ''[[House of Mouse]]''. In the latter show, he is the co-owner of Mickey's nightclub. He is part of the ensemble cast of characters in the TV show ''[[Mickey Mouse Clubhouse]]'' as well. He also appears in the 2013 ''[[Mickey Mouse (TV series)|Mickey Mouse]]'' TV shorts for Disney Channel and its [[Disney+]] successor, [[The Wonderful World of Mickey Mouse|''The Wondeful World of Mickey Mouse'']]. Donald also appears in the ''[[DuckTales (2017 TV series)|DuckTales]]'' reboot, in which he is a main character as opposed to his minor role in the original cartoon. The series depicts him as having once been Scrooge's partner in adventure along with his sister [[Della Duck|Della]]. However, ten years prior to the series' beginning, Della went missing, leading to Donald and Scrooge going their separate ways and not speaking to each other throughout that time. In the present, Donald reluctantly brings Della's sons and his legal charges, the triplets, to Scrooge's mansion so he can babysit them while Donald attends a job interview, though he still has not forgiven Scrooge for their past history. Donald is temporarily hired by Scrooge's rival [[Flintheart Glomgold]] and ends up at the city of Atlantis, where Scrooge has also brought the boys. After some initial conflict Scrooge offers to let them stay with him in his mansion. Donald owns a boat in the series, which is relocated to Scrooge's pool at the conclusion of the series premiere. Later in the series, it is revealed that Donald's anger is the result of a fear that no one can understand him, though with the help of an anger management counselor and while taking care of Huey, Dewey, Louie, he was able to channel it into protective instinct. === Voice actors === [[File:Clarence Nash and Tony Anselmo.jpg|thumb|Tony Anselmo and Clarence Nash]] Donald's first voice was performed by [[Clarence Nash]], who voiced him for 50 years.{{cite news|first=Jim|last=Korkis|title=Becoming Donald Duck: The Clarence Nash Story|url=https://www.mouseplanet.com/10730/Becoming_Donald_Duck_The_Clarence_Nash_Story|date=June 25, 2014|publisher=Mouseplanet|access-date=November 8, 2017}} As long as Nash was alive no one else was permitted to do Donald's voice. Nash voiced Donald for the last time in ''[[Mickey's Christmas Carol]]'' (1983), making him the only character in the film to be voiced by his original voice actor.{{cite web|url=https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/shorts/Mickeys-Christmas-Carol/|title=Mickey's Christmas Carol (1983)|website=Behind The Voice Actors|language=en-US|access-date=2025-12-01|archive-date=December 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211210070059/https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/shorts/Mickeys-Christmas-Carol/|url-status=live}} He continued to provide Donald's voice for commercials, promos, and other miscellaneous material until his death in 1985.
